protocol.item: ACUTE LIVER FAILURE IN THE ED
protocol.source_text:
ACUTE LIVER FAILURE IN THE ED 
 
Definition 
 
Rapid development of severe acute liver injury characterised by impaired synthetic function  
(INR ³ 1.5) and complicated by the development of encephalopathy, in a person without a history of liver 
disease or who had well-compensated liver disease. 
 
Causes (DAVES) 
 
• Drugs (paracetamol, TB drugs, ARVs, NSAIDs, traditional medicine, illicit drugs) 
• Alcohol 
• Viral (Hep A, B, C, E; EBV; CMV; HSV; HZV, ParvoB19) 
• Extras (acute fatty liver of pregnancy, HELLP, ischaemic necrosis, vascular, metabolic, autoimmune, 
Wilson’s disease, Budd-Chiari, idiopathic, heatstroke, Reye’s, malignancy 
• Sepsis 
 
Clinical features of Acute Liver Failure 
 
History 
Clinical signs on examination of ALF 
Ø Date of onset of symptoms 
Ø Travel history 
Ø Drug use – prescription and illicit 
Ø Alcohol use 
Ø Herbal or traditional medication use 
Ø Target symptoms consistent with the 
presenting complication 
Ø Exposure to a viral illness (sexual contacts, 
body piercing) 
Ø Jaundice 
Ø RUQ tenderness 
Ø Hepatomegaly 
Ø Splenomegaly 
Ø Ascites 
Ø Evidence of bleeding 
Ø Evidence of infection 
Ø Asterixis (hepatic flap) 
Ø Evidence of encephalopathy 
 
 Grading of Hepatic Encephalopathy (HE) 
Grade 
Intellectual Function 
Neuromuscular Function 
I 
Impaired attention, irritable, depressed, personality 
changes 
Tremor, apraxia, incoordination 
II 
Drowsy, poor memory, behavioural changes, sleep 
disturbances 
Asterixis, ataxia, slow slurred 
speech 
III 
Confusion, somnolence, disorientation, amnesia 
Hypoactive reflexes, clonus, 
nystagmus, muscle rigidity 
IV 
Stupor, coma 
Dilated pupils, decerebtrate 
posture, oculocephalic reflex 
 
 
Dr R Gihwala CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020  
Contents

 
Complications and Clinical Manifestations 
 
Patients in ALF tend to present to the ED with complications that may include any of the following listed in 
the box. 
 
Complications and clinical manifestations of acute liver failure 
Ø Neurological 
• Hepatic encephalopathy 
• Cerebral oedema 
• Seizures 
• Raised ICP 
Ø Coagulopathy and bleeding 
Ø Metabolic 
• Hypoglycaemia 
• Hyponatraemia 
• Hypokalaemia 
• Hypophosphataemia 
• Lactic acidosis  
• Hyperammonaemia 
Ø Infection 
• Septicaemia 
• Peritonitis 
• Pneumonia 
• Urinary tract sepsis 
Ø Respiratory 
• Hypoxia 
• Aspiration 
• ARDS (non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema) 
Ø Cardiovascular 
• Hypotension  
• Hypertension (raised ICP) 
Ø Renal failure 
 
 
General Management Approach Goals 
Ø Identification of the aetiology of the ALF whenever possible and initiation of specific treatment 
Ø Supportive and symptomatic management of ALF with timely transfer to a critical care unit 
Ø Early consultation with Liver Transplant specialists 
 
Emergency Department Management 
 
Immediate management 
• Resuscitate and stabilize ABCs, blood glucose, oxygen if hypoxic and establish IV access. 
• Intubate and ventilate if unresponsive (normal glucose) from HE (RSI to preven
